video_title: How to Spot Exceptional Talent Before Everyone Else
gist: a16z partners (including twins Olivia and Justine Moore, plus 'David' and 'Eric') unveil Cosign, a new AI-populated professional-reputation directory built on granular public/private endorsements ('who shaped your career', 'who you'd work with in the trenches', 'person to watch'), arguing that peer cosigns are becoming a more valuable and scarce signal than credentials or LinkedIn connections, especially as AI-driven outreach floods inboxes. Note: despite the title, the episode is a product-launch conversation about Cosign rather than a general talent-scouting how-to.

insights.claim: a16z is launching Cosign, a directory-style platform for professional reputation built on peer endorsements rather than institutional credentials, framed around the idea that being publicly followed/endorsed by figures like Patrick Collison, Elon Musk, or Marc Andreessen now signals more than a Stanford degree.
insights.speaker: Eric (a16z, introducing Cosign)
insights.so_what: Signals a broader shift toward peer-endorsement graphs as a credentialing layer; relevant for anyone building identity, recruiting, or reputation infrastructure.
insights.quote: What's more impressive to you? Someone who went to Stanford or someone who is followed by Patrick Collison, Elon Musk, Mark Andre.

insights.claim: Cosign's profile schema requires at least three endorsement types per person: who shaped your career (mentor), who you'd work with 'in the trenches,' and who is a 'person to watch' for future success — designed to be built up and rank-ordered over years, similar to how an investor track record accrues credibility.
insights.speaker: Eric (a16z, Cosign product)
insights.so_what: A reusable schema for any reputation or credentialing product: separate mentor-signal, trust-signal, and forward-looking-conviction-signal rather than a single undifferentiated 'connection'.

insights.claim: Cosign is designed to solve the cold-start problem of reputation networks by using AI to scrape and structure already-public information (funding announcements, X/Twitter posts and quote-tweets) into pre-populated profiles, rather than requiring users to opt in first, including a live feed sourced from a direct data connection into X.
insights.speaker: David/Eric (a16z, Cosign product)
insights.so_what: AI-driven aggregation of public data is becoming a substitute for organic network effects, lowering the bar for launching reputation/social-graph products that would otherwise face a cold start.
insights.quote: only you know because of AI can we generate all of this information on people and like recreate you know a professional graph

insights.claim: Cosign is deliberately built to be all-positive, an explicit product trade-off ('no product can be all things to all people'), betting that people will use it to showcase real achievements rather than adding another venue for critique, which the team believes already has plenty of outlets online.
insights.speaker: David (a16z, Cosign product)
insights.so_what: A specific, falsifiable product bet worth tracking: whether a purely positive-sentiment social feed can sustain daily engagement versus mixed-sentiment incumbents like X and LinkedIn.
insights.quote: this product is going to win on people um using it to show off like to show off in a good way

insights.claim: Cosign's core differentiation thesis is that valuable reputation signal (compliments, endorsements, career-defining moments) currently happens ephemerally on X and disappears within a day, and that permanently attaching those moments to a durable professional profile is itself the product's main value-add versus existing social feeds.
insights.speaker: Eric (a16z, Cosign product)
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific unmet need — persistence of social proof — that competing 'reputation layer' or 'social CV' startups could also target.
insights.quote: any uh announcement is going to be tied to their sort of, you know, durable reputation.

insights.claim: Cosign is positioned as a free alternative to paid deal/company databases like Crunchbase and PitchBook, viable specifically because a16z can subsidize it as a community good for the startup ecosystem rather than needing it to be a standalone profitable business on its own.
insights.speaker: Eric (a16z, Cosign product)
insights.so_what: A large platform/fund subsidizing a free data product can undercut paid incumbents in adjacent categories — a competitive dynamic worth watching for Crunchbase/PitchBook's moat.
insights.quote: and free, you know, crunching base, pitchbook, you know, cost [clears throat] money, etc. They're great products, they have to be businesses, but we have the luxury of being able to just really offer this for the startup community.

themes.theme: Information asymmetry in talent and capital markets

insights.claim: A speaker who has invested for nearly a decade argues that 'the most valuable data in all of Silicon Valley' is knowing who has genuine conviction about a person, and that even professional investors must manually canvass their networks daily asking whether anyone has worked with a given person because no structured signal for this currently exists.
insights.speaker: guest investor (a16z)
insights.so_what: Names a large, currently unpriced information-asymmetry problem in talent/capital allocation that a structured endorsement product like Cosign is explicitly trying to capture.
insights.quote: the most valuable data in all of Silicon Valley is like who has conviction

insights.claim: As AI-driven outreach and browser-automation agents lower the cost of applying to jobs, a single hiring post is already generating around 2,000 responses and is expected to scale to roughly 10,000 within a month and 100,000 soon after, making manual (or even AI-assisted) filtering increasingly infeasible.
insights.speaker: Olivia Moore (a16z)
insights.so_what: Rising volumes of AI-generated candidate/lead outreach make trusted human curation layers scarcer and more valuable, not less — a thesis relevant to recruiting-tech and lead-gen investing.
insights.quote: it's going to be 2,000 now and it's going to be 10,000 you know a month from now as browser usage gets better and more people use browser it's going to be 100,000

insights.claim: Early, public endorsements compound in value for the endorser as much as the endorsed: a founder who becomes successful will disproportionately route future business (fundraises, hires, intros) back to whoever backed or endorsed them first and publicly, before anyone else did.
insights.speaker: David/Eric (a16z)
insights.so_what: Reframes public endorsement as a low-cost, convex-payoff strategy resembling early-stage investing, but accessible to non-investors and non-founders alike.
insights.quote: people always remember like by order of magnitude more the people who believed in them first

insights.claim: Paul Graham's 2009 public claim that Sam Altman was among the five best entrepreneurs he'd encountered (made before Altman had a major exit) is cited as the canonical example of an early cosign compounding into an outsized career trajectory, with Altman going on to run Y Combinator and later build a major company.
insights.speaker: David (a16z)
insights.so_what: A concrete historical case study for how a single credible public endorsement can materially accelerate a founder's trajectory.
insights.quote: Paul Graham co-signed Sam Alman famously uh I feel like 2009 or something he said like the five best entrepreneurs

insights.claim: Ryan Hoover (founder of Product Hunt) publicly cosigning 'Eric' early in his career and bringing him on to help build Product Hunt's community is presented as a direct real-world case of an endorsement from a builder launching someone into an influential industry role.
insights.speaker: David (a16z)
insights.so_what: Illustrates that reputation-transfer effects apply broadly across community/product roles, not just founders and investors.
insights.quote: Ryan Hoover who was founder of product hunt co-signed Eric and brought Eric on to become one of the leaders of building the community

insights.claim: Russell Kaplan, now president at Cognition, was flagged as a 'person to watch' seven years ago in an informal talent-scouting email experiment, at a time when he was a 22-year-old engineer at Tesla — illustrating that peer conviction signals can have real predictive value years before a person's status becomes widely recognized.
insights.speaker: Eric (a16z)
insights.so_what: A concrete validated example that early peer-conviction signals can predict career trajectory well ahead of public consensus, supporting the thesis behind Cosign.
insights.quote: One of them was Russell Kaplan who's now the president at Cognition. And he was like a 22-year-old just engineer at Tesla.

insights.claim: There is an inherent incentive tension in reputation-sharing: insiders are reluctant to publicly cosign genuinely great, undiscovered people because doing so gives up proprietary 'alpha'; the reframe offered is that the person worth publicly cosigning isn't the one raising a round right now, but the one who will raise a much bigger round years later and remember who backed them first.
insights.speaker: Eric/David (a16z)
insights.so_what: Articulates the actual incentive-design problem any reputation or endorsement marketplace must solve to get high-signal contributors to participate honestly and early.
insights.quote: if that person's raising a preede round right now and you want to do it, don't cosign them right now, but you the person you want to to cosign is the one that's raising a preede round two years from now

themes.theme: Under-30 talent reshaping tech and AI

insights.claim: The speakers argue several of the most consequential current figures in tech/AI are in their mid-20s with unconventional paths: a 25-year-old podcaster (rendered in the transcript as 'Doresh') who has never held a formal job and built influence purely through interviews and cosigns from established figures, alongside young founders and researchers in their mid-to-late 20s running some of the most important AI companies and labs.
insights.speaker: David/Eric (a16z)
insights.so_what: Supports a sourcing thesis that founder/researcher age and traditional pedigree are weaker predictors than peer endorsement — relevant to how early-stage investors should prioritize network-based discovery over credential screens.
insights.quote: one of the most important intellectuals right now is Doresh he's 25 years old he's never had a job as far as I'm aware he just you know came to San Francisco started podcasting

insights.claim: A media/commentary voice (rendered in the transcript as 'Py McCormack,' known for deep-tech and 'vertical integrator' commentary) has curated a public list of roughly 37 companies as the ones to join to break into that space, illustrating how a non-founder, non-investor can still function as a de facto cosign of reputational capital that directs both talent and attention.
insights.speaker: David (a16z)
insights.so_what: Shows that curated public lists from credible commentators function as an alternate, capital-free distribution channel for reputation and hiring signal in a specific niche (deep tech).
insights.quote: Paky's got 37 companies that he's chosen. He says these are the companies if you want to get into one into the space.

insights.claim: A former early LinkedIn employee describes the company's founding growth sequence as 'growth, usage, revenue': first maximize network size and give value even to passive sign-ups, then build usage-driving products on top of the network substrate (such as LinkedIn Jobs), and only later focus on monetization — a staged framework being echoed in Cosign's own rollout approach.
insights.speaker: Josh (a16z, ex-LinkedIn)
insights.so_what: A reusable staged prioritization template (network size before feature depth before monetization) for any network-effects startup's early roadmap.

insights.claim: Early LinkedIn built a 'social resume' concept — surfacing not just a candidate's profile but who within the hiring company or network could vouch for or add context on them — which is described as a materially higher-value hiring primitive than a flat resume, but one LinkedIn has since drifted away from as connections became low-trust ('we met once at a party, we high-fived').
insights.speaker: Josh (a16z, ex-LinkedIn)
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, previously-built-then-abandoned feature (contextualized, vouched-for hiring) as reopened whitespace for a reputation-focused challenger product.
insights.quote: we met once at a party. We high-fived. We had a good email exchange.

insights.claim: LinkedIn's durable network effect is explained as resting on a large, mostly-passive user base — people who are 'mildly happily employed,' signed up once, and rarely engage but remain reachable for the right opportunity — versus a smaller, highly active minority (sales, BD, recruiting, venture) who use it constantly; this split is framed as the reason a ~20-year network with over a billion users has proven very hard to displace.
insights.speaker: Josh (a16z, ex-LinkedIn)
insights.so_what: Explains structurally why 'LinkedIn killers' keep failing and suggests a challenger should position as a complementary reputation layer rather than a full replacement.
insights.quote: We used to talk about the like mildly happily employed

insights.claim: LinkedIn's practical defensibility against being scraped or cloned rests on best-in-class bot detection and dense network switching costs, even though entire third-party businesses already exist purely to scrape and resell LinkedIn data.
insights.speaker: David (a16z)
insights.so_what: Explains why data-replication alone is not a viable strategy for challenging LinkedIn; a challenger needs a distinct data source (e.g., public/AI-aggregated reputation) rather than scraped LinkedIn data.
insights.quote: they are famously good at bot detection

insights.claim: Vertical-specific 'niche LinkedIns' can out-compete the general LinkedIn network for a specific community — GitHub is cited as already functioning as a better professional-reputation layer for engineers than LinkedIn itself.
insights.speaker: David (a16z)
insights.so_what: Suggests reputation/identity startups may win by targeting a specific professional vertical rather than competing with LinkedIn head-on.
insights.quote: GitHub is arguably a better LinkedIn for engineers than than LinkedIn itself.

insights.claim: A roughly 12-year-old (circa-2014) public call from investor Charles Hudson that it was 'time to disrupt' LinkedIn is cited as evidence that, despite many well-funded attempts (including some a16z itself backed) and even crypto-incentive approaches, no product has meaningfully dented LinkedIn's position.
insights.speaker: David (a16z)
insights.so_what: A concrete historical marker showing how durable professional-network effects have been against a decade-plus of competitive attempts, tempering expectations for any new challenger including Cosign.
insights.quote: Charles Hudson uh you know great great investor like you know 12 years ago was a blog post like where are the LinkedIn competitors it's time to disrupt

insights.claim: LinkedIn's 2016 acquisition by Microsoft for roughly $26 billion is referenced in passing as evidence of the platform's scale and status as one of the most iconic and lucrative products in tech, underscoring how high the bar is for any would-be successor.
insights.speaker: David/Josh (a16z)
insights.so_what: Sets the scale benchmark ($26B) against which any professional-network challenger's ambitions should be measured.
insights.quote: when they when they got acquired cuz like what only 26 billion?

insights.claim: AngelList a decade ago 'owned the investor graph' as a genuinely public, free directory tying together startup companies, investors, and talent, but a series of subsequent strategic bets shifted its focus toward monetized private tooling and away from that free public network — a specific abandoned position that Cosign is now explicitly trying to re-occupy.
insights.speaker: Eric/David (a16z)
insights.so_what: Suggests a repeatable pattern: public directory/network products that pivot toward monetized private tooling leave a reoccupiable public layer for a new entrant — worth watching whether Cosign or a rival actually captures it.
insights.quote: when they owned the investor graph and really really it was for the startup community and it was really focused around you know companies investors and talent

themes.theme: Silicon Valley's 'pay-it-forward' culture as structural advantage

insights.claim: The speakers argue Silicon Valley's competitive advantage over other industries is a self-reinforcing 'pay it forward' culture where senior people stake their own reputational capital on unproven newcomers, and that this social mechanism — not just capital availability — is what lets people without prior credentials rise quickly; Cosign is framed as an attempt to formalize and scale that existing cultural pattern rather than invent a new one.
insights.speaker: David/Eric (a16z)
insights.so_what: Frames the addressable opportunity for reputation-network products as codifying an existing informal cultural mechanism rather than creating new behavior, which may lower adoption risk.
insights.quote: Silicon Valley and the tech industry is so special for this kind of pay it forward for this belief in somebody

insights.claim: Beyond founders, the team explicitly wants to give reputational credit to under-recognized company-builders (designers, engineers, marketers, product managers), and plans to revive a discontinued 'Rise Awards' program (originally run around 2015-2016, which drew thousands of submissions) specifically to recognize non-founder operators whose contributions currently aren't portable when they leave to join or start new companies.
insights.speaker: David/Eric (a16z)
insights.so_what: Identifies individual contributors/operators as an underserved segment for reputation products — a target market not well served by founder- or investor-centric platforms like AngelList or Crunchbase.
insights.quote: It takes so many great designers and engineers and marketers and product managers
